learn.hook: Before big factories with chimneys, cloth for the world market was spun and woven in village cottages, with merchants running from hut to hut!
points: Proto-industrialisation was the phase before factories, when there was large-scale production for an international market that was not based in factories. It is seen in England and Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries.

Merchants moved to the countryside because in towns powerful crafts and trade guilds controlled production, regulated prices and competition, and kept new people out. Peasants and artisans in villages, short of land and income, welcomed merchants' advances to produce goods.

A merchant clothier bought wool from a wool stapler and took it to spinners; the yarn then went to weavers, fullers and dyers, and the cloth was finished in London before export. Merchants, not the workers, controlled the whole chain.

Factories grew in England from the late 18th century. Imports of raw cotton rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds by 1787. Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill, and James Watt improved Newcomen's steam engine and patented his new engine in 1781; Matthew Boulton manufactured it.

Change was slow. In Victorian Britain labour was cheap and plentiful, so many industrialists preferred hand labour, especially in seasonal industries. The upper classes valued handmade goods as a sign of refinement. When James Hargreaves' spinning jenny (1764) came in, women who survived on hand spinning attacked the new machines.

example.q: Think it through: Why did many Victorian industrialists prefer workers to machines?
steps: Machines were costly to buy and repair, and they often broke down.
There was no shortage of poor workers willing to work for low wages.
Many industries were seasonal, so employers wanted workers only for part of the year.
Hand labour also gave the variety and fine finish that rich buyers wanted.
example.answer: Labour was cheap and plentiful, machines were costly and inflexible, and many buyers wanted handmade goods.

learn.reallife: Today, handloom saris from Banaras, Kanchipuram or Pochampally are still prized because they are handmade, just as rich Victorians valued handmade goods.

quiz.q: What does 'proto-industrialisation' refer to?
options: Large-scale production for an international market before the factory age
Making goods only for one's own family
Industries set up after the Second World War
Production of goods only in big factories
quiz.explain: Proto means early or first. It was large-scale production for international markets, done in homes and workshops, not factories.
quiz.mistake: Thinks industrialisation always means factories

quiz.q: Why did merchants in 17th and 18th century Europe find it hard to expand production in towns?
options: Powerful crafts and trade guilds controlled production and kept new people out
Towns had no workers at all
quiz.explain: Guilds trained craftspeople, regulated prices and competition and restricted entry, often with monopoly rights from rulers.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the role of guilds

quiz.q: Who controlled the whole cloth-making chain in proto-industrial England?
quiz.explain: The merchant clothier bought wool, paid spinners, weavers, fullers and dyers, and sold the finished cloth, so he controlled production.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the workers or the wool seller controlled production

quiz.q: Imports of raw cotton into Britain rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to how many million pounds by 1787?
quiz.explain: Raw cotton imports soared to 22 million pounds, showing how fast the cotton industry was growing.
quiz.mistake: Does not recall the scale of growth

quiz.q: Who created the cotton mill?
quiz.explain: Arkwright's mill brought all processes under one roof and management. Watt improved the steam engine; Ford built cars much later.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the inventors of the period

quiz.q: In which year did James Watt patent his improved steam engine?
quiz.explain: Watt patented it in 1781. 1764 is the spinning jenny, and 1854 is Bombay's first cotton mill.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the spinning jenny or other dates

quiz.q: Why did women in the woollen industry attack the spinning jenny?
options: They survived on hand spinning and feared losing their jobs
quiz.explain: The jenny let one worker turn many spindles at once, which threatened the livelihood of hand spinners.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the link between machines and unemployment

quiz.q: Why did upper classes in Victorian Britain prefer handmade goods?
options: Only handmade goods could be exported
Machines had not been invented yet
They saw them as a symbol of refinement and class
quiz.explain: Handmade products were finely finished and individually designed, so the rich valued them; machine-made goods went largely to the colonies.
quiz.mistake: Assumes everyone wanted cheap machine goods

teach.praise: Fabulous! Village homes worked for world markets, long before factories!
teach.nudge: Who ran production before factories, and why didn't they do it in towns?

learn.hook: Indian cotton and silk once dressed the world. Then came Manchester's machine cloth, and later India's own mills fought back.
points: Before machine industries, Indian silk and cotton dominated the international textile market. Ports like Surat on the Gujarat coast, Masulipatam on the Coromandel coast and Hoogly in Bengal linked India with the world. As the East India Company gained power, new ports at Bombay and Calcutta grew.

The Company appointed paid servants called gomasthas to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine the quality of cloth. Weavers who took advances could not sell to other buyers, and clashes broke out in many villages in Carnatic and Bengal.

In the 19th century, British cotton goods flooded India. Indian weavers lost export markets, their local market shrank, and raw cotton became costly when the American Civil War (1860s) made Britain buy more Indian cotton.

The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in 1854; the first jute mill in Bengal in 1855; the first spinning and weaving mill of Madras began production in 1874. Early entrepreneurs included Dwarkanath Tagore in Bengal and Parsis like Dinshaw Petit and Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee Tata in Bombay. The Tata Iron and Steel works began production at Jamshedpur in 1912, and Seth Hukumchand set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in 1917.

Mills hired workers through jobbers, often trusted old workers who brought people from their villages but later demanded gifts and controlled their lives. Industry grew with the Swadeshi movement's boycott of foreign cloth and during the First World War, when Manchester imports fell and Indian mills supplied army needs. Handloom production also survived and grew, helped by the fly shuttle.

example.q: Think it through: How did the First World War help Indian factories grow?
steps: British mills were busy producing for war needs, so exports of Manchester cloth to India fell.
Indian mills suddenly had a large home market to supply.
They also got orders for army needs: jute bags, cloth for uniforms, tents, leather boots and saddles.
Production grew so much that Manchester never fully regained its old position in India.
example.answer: Manchester imports fell and Indian mills supplied war needs, so they expanded and gained the home market.

learn.reallife: Jamshedpur in Jharkhand, named after Jamsetji Tata, grew into a big industrial city around the steel works that began production in 1912.

quiz.q: Who were gomasthas?
options: Paid servants of the East India Company who supervised weavers and checked cloth quality
Village headmen who collected land revenue
quiz.explain: Gomasthas supervised weavers, collected supplies and examined quality, and often treated weavers harshly.
quiz.mistake: Confuses gomasthas with jobbers or mill owners

quiz.q: Which pre-colonial port was on the Coromandel coast?
quiz.explain: Masulipatam was on the Coromandel coast, Surat on the Gujarat coast and Hoogly in Bengal. Bombay grew later under the Company.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the locations of the ports

quiz.q: Why did raw cotton become costly for Indian weavers in the 1860s?
options: The American Civil War cut cotton supplies from the US, so Britain bought more Indian cotton
The monsoon failed for ten years
quiz.explain: With US cotton cut off, Britain turned to India, and Indian raw cotton exports rose, pushing up prices for local weavers.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect a world event with Indian prices

quiz.q: In which year did the first cotton mill come up in Bombay?
quiz.explain: Bombay's first cotton mill came up in 1854. 1874 is Madras, 1912 is Tata steel and 1917 is Hukumchand's jute mill.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the dates of different industrial milestones

quiz.q: Who set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in 1917?
quiz.explain: Seth Hukumchand, a Marwari businessman, set up the first Indian-owned jute mill in Calcutta in 1917.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the early Indian industrialists

quiz.q: Where did the Tata Iron and Steel works begin production in 1912?
quiz.explain: The Tata Iron and Steel works began production at Jamshedpur in 1912. The town is named after Jamsetji Tata, who planned the steel works.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all early industry was in Bombay

quiz.q: Who was a jobber in Indian mills?
options: A merchant who exported yarn to China
A trusted worker who recruited people from villages for the mill
A worker who changed jobs often
quiz.explain: Jobbers brought workers from their villages and helped them settle, but over time gained power and demanded gifts.
quiz.mistake: Takes the word 'jobber' at face value

quiz.q: How did the First World War help Indian industries?
options: It made Manchester cloth cheaper in India
It ended all trade with Britain forever
Manchester imports fell and Indian mills supplied war needs like uniforms and tents
quiz.explain: With British mills busy for the war, Indian mills gained the home market and army orders, and grew rapidly.
quiz.mistake: Assumes wars only harm industry

teach.praise: Super! Indian weavers struggled, but Indian mills rose with swadeshi and the war.

learn.hook: Making cloth is one thing; making people want to buy it is another. Welcome to the world of labels, calendars and advertisements!
points: New producers had to win buyers. Advertisements make products seem desirable and necessary, and try to shape people's minds and create new needs.
Manchester industrialists put labels on cloth bundles. Words like 'MADE IN MANCHESTER' in bold letters were meant to make buyers trust the quality.

Labels also carried images and beautiful pictures. Indian gods and goddesses, such as Krishna or Saraswati, appeared on labels so the product seemed to have divine approval and felt familiar to Indian buyers.

Manufacturers printed calendars to popularise their products. Unlike newspapers, calendars were used even by people who could not read, and they hung all year in tea shops, homes and offices. Images of historical figures such as emperors and nawabs were also used to give products a sense of respect and tradition.
When Indian manufacturers advertised, the nationalist message was clear: if you care for the nation, buy products that Indians produce. Advertisements became a vehicle for the swadeshi idea.

example.q: Think it through: Why did manufacturers choose calendars rather than only newspaper ads?
steps: Many people in India at that time could not read newspapers.
A calendar is useful, so people kept it on the wall for the whole year.
It was seen daily in tea shops, homes and offices.
So the product's picture and name reached people every day, even those who could not read.
example.answer: Calendars were used all year and seen daily, even by people who could not read, so the brand stayed in front of them.

learn.reallife: Look around a kirana shop or a dhaba today: free calendars with company logos and festival images are still a popular way to advertise.

quiz.q: What is the main aim of an advertisement?
options: To make a product appear desirable and necessary
To stop people from buying anything new
To reduce the price of the product
To tell people the product is useless
quiz.explain: Advertisements try to shape people's minds and create new needs so that buyers want the product.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ads only give neutral information

quiz.q: Why did Manchester industrialists print 'MADE IN MANCHESTER' on cloth labels?
options: To make the cloth look cheaper
To make buyers confident about the quality of the cloth
To show the cloth was handmade in India
quiz.explain: The place-name, printed in bold, told buyers the cloth came from a famous industrial centre, making them trust its quality.
quiz.mistake: Does not see labels as a marketing tool

quiz.q: Why did some labels carry images of Indian gods and goddesses?
options: To ban the product in temples
To suggest divine approval and make the product feel familiar to buyers
Because the cloth was made in temples
quiz.explain: Images like Krishna or Saraswati made the foreign product seem trustworthy and familiar to Indian buyers.
quiz.mistake: Takes the images literally instead of as a selling strategy

quiz.q: Why were calendars an effective way to advertise?
options: They were only for rich people
They were used even by people who could not read and hung on walls all year
quiz.explain: Calendars stayed on walls in homes, tea shops and offices for a whole year, so people saw the product daily.
quiz.mistake: Thinks advertising works only through written words

quiz.q: Why were images of emperors and nawabs used in advertisements?
options: To give the product a sense of respect and tradition
To show who made the product
quiz.explain: Historical figures suggested that the product was as respected as royalty and connected to a proud past.
quiz.mistake: Does not see images as carrying a message

quiz.q: What message did Indian manufacturers often put in their advertisements?
options: If you care for the nation, buy products that Indians produce
quiz.explain: Indian advertisements carried the swadeshi idea, linking buying Indian goods with love for the nation.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Indian and British advertising messages

quiz.q: Where did printed calendars with product advertisements commonly hang?
options: Only in government offices in London
In tea shops, homes and offices
quiz.explain: Calendars were cheap and useful, so they were seen in everyday places by ordinary people.
quiz.mistake: Does not know who the calendars were aimed at

quiz.q: Which idea did advertisements by Indian manufacturers help spread?
quiz.explain: By urging people to buy Indian goods, advertisements became a vehicle of the swadeshi message.
quiz.mistake: Confuses advertising messages with other ideas in the syllabus

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'How did companies get people to buy their cloth? Did they shout in the bazaar?'
teach.praise: Smart! Labels, calendars and pictures made people want to buy.
